records.greek: Ἀμὴν ἀμὴν λέγω ὑμῖν, ὁ μὴ εἰσερχόμενος διὰ τῆς θύρας εἰς τὴν αὐλὴν τῶν προβάτων ἀλλὰ ἀναβαίνων ἀλλαχόθεν ἐκεῖνος κλέπτης ἐστὶν καὶ λῃστής·
records.gloss: "Truly truly I say to you, the [one] not entering through the door into the fold of the sheep but going up from elsewhere, that one a thief is and a bandit;

L.1: "Truly, truly I say to you, the one who does not enter through the door into the fold of the sheep, but climbs up from elsewhere, that one is a thief and a bandit.

R.1: "I tell you the truth: anyone who does not go into the sheep pen through the door, but climbs over the wall somewhere else, is a thief and a bandit.

decisions.choice: the speech goes straight on from 9:41: "you" are the Pharisees of 9:40-41
alternatives: a new speech to a new audience
decisions.reason: There is no change of place, time or listeners between 9:41 and 10:1; the chapter division is later than the text. Jesus has just told the Pharisees who claim to see that their sin remains (9:41), and he goes on speaking to them (10:6 says he spoke "to them"). The picture of the shepherd and the thieves follows directly on their treatment of the man who was healed and thrown out (9:34).

decisions.choice: the fold: a walled enclosure for sheep with a single entrance
alternatives: the courtyard of a house only
decisions.reason: The word means an enclosed yard. Sheepfolds were enclosures with walls of stone, often topped with thorns, and one opening; sometimes the yard of a house served. The sheep were kept there at night. Anyone who came in over the wall instead of through the entrance had no right to be there. The same word is used for the courtyard of the high priest (18:15).

decisions.choice: thief: one who steals by stealth; bandit: one who robs by violence
alternatives: two words for the same person with no difference
decisions.reason: The two words are not the same. The first is the ordinary word for a thief, used of Judas (12:6). The second is a robber who uses force, the kind who attacked travelers on the road (Luke 10:30); it is also the word for Barabbas (18:40), and in the first century it was used of armed rebels. Together they describe someone who takes what is not his, by cunning or by force.

decisions.choice: the shepherd picture draws on Ezekiel 34, Jeremiah 23:1-4 and Psalm 23
decisions.reason: The Scriptures often call Israel God's flock and its leaders shepherds. Ezekiel 34 condemns the shepherds of Israel who fed themselves and scattered the sheep, and promises that God himself will seek his sheep and set one shepherd, his servant David, over them (Ezekiel 34:11-16, 23). Jeremiah 23:1-4 pronounces woe on shepherds who destroy and scatter the flock. Psalm 23 calls God the shepherd who leads his sheep to pasture. That the thieves and bandits here are meant as the false shepherds of Ezekiel 34, in the persons of the Pharisees who threw the man out (9:34), is likely from the setting but not stated; the verbal links are clearer in 10:11-16.

decisions.choice: Truly, truly I say to you (L); Truly, truly, I tell you (B); I tell you the truth (R)
decisions.reason: The book-wide rendering for John (see 1:51), recorded once in this passage; it covers 10:7 as well.

decisions.choice: the fold of the sheep (L); the sheepfold (B); the sheep pen (R); a thief and a bandit at every level
decisions.reason: "Bandit" keeps the two Greek words distinct (meaning decision m3) and is used again in 10:8. "Door" is kept at every level so that "I am the door" (10:7, 9) is heard as the same word.

decisions.choice: climbs over the wall somewhere else
decisions.reason: Readable says plainly what climbing in "from elsewhere" means in a walled fold (meaning decision m2).

records.heading: The shepherd and the sheep

records.greek: ὁ δὲ εἰσερχόμενος διὰ τῆς θύρας ποιμήν ἐστιν τῶν προβάτων.
records.gloss: The [one] but entering through the door shepherd is of the sheep.

L.2: But the one who enters through the door is [the] shepherd of the sheep.

R.2: But the one who goes in through the door is the shepherd of the sheep.

decisions.choice: shepherd without the article: he is the one with a right to the sheep, the shepherd as opposed to a thief
alternatives: the one Good Shepherd already named
decisions.reason: The Greek has no article with "shepherd". The point is the contrast with verse 1: whoever comes by the door shows himself a shepherd, not a thief. At this stage of the picture the shepherd is not yet identified; Jesus names himself the good shepherd in 10:11.

decisions.choice: entering through the door: coming openly by the rightful way
alternatives: a reference to Jesus as the door (10:7)
decisions.reason: In the picture the door is simply the proper entrance, opened for the shepherd by the doorkeeper (verse 3). Only in 10:7 does Jesus apply the door to himself, in a second step of the picture.

decisions.choice: [the] shepherd
decisions.reason: Literal brackets the article English needs (meaning decision m1).

records.greek: τούτῳ ὁ θυρωρὸς ἀνοίγει, καὶ τὰ πρόβατα τῆς φωνῆς αὐτοῦ ἀκούει καὶ τὰ ἴδια πρόβατα φωνεῖ κατ’ ὄνομα καὶ ἐξάγει αὐτά.
records.gloss: To this [one] the doorkeeper opens, and the sheep the voice of him hear, and the own sheep he calls by name and leads out them.

L.3: For this one the doorkeeper opens, and the sheep hear his voice, and he calls his own sheep by name and leads them out.

R.3: The one who keeps watch at the door opens it for him, and the sheep listen to his voice. He calls each of his own sheep by name and leads them out.

decisions.choice: the doorkeeper: a watchman who guarded the entrance of the fold
alternatives: a figure for some particular person
decisions.reason: Where several flocks shared one fold for the night, a watchman kept the entrance and opened it in the morning to the shepherds he knew. The doorkeeper is part of the scene and is not explained in the passage; nothing in the text says whom he stands for.

decisions.choice: his own sheep: his flock among others in the same fold
alternatives: all the sheep in the fold
decisions.reason: The phrase "his own" sets his sheep apart from others kept in the fold. He calls each of his own by name, and those are the ones he leads out (10:14, 27).

decisions.choice: hear his voice: listen and respond to him
decisions.reason: Hearing a voice in John is responding to the one who speaks (5:25; 10:16, 27; 18:37). The sheep know whose voice it is and answer it.

decisions.choice: leads out: perhaps an echo of God leading his people out of Egypt and of Numbers 27:17
alternatives: an ordinary word for taking sheep out to pasture, with no echo
decisions.reason: The verb is the ordinary one for leading out. In the Greek Old Testament it is used of God bringing Israel out of Egypt (Exodus 20:2) and in Moses's prayer for a leader who will lead the people out and bring them in, so that they are not like sheep without a shepherd (Numbers 27:16-17). Whether John intends the echo here is uncertain.

decisions.choice: his, he, him for the shepherd in 10:1-5 written without a deity_pronoun span; pronouns for Jesus from 10:6 on take one
alternatives: capitalisable pronouns for the shepherd in the picture
decisions.reason: In 10:1-5 Jesus tells a picture (10:6), and the shepherd is a figure in it, like the bridegroom of 3:29; his pronouns are not pronouns for God or Christ. When Jesus applies the picture to himself from 10:7 ("I am the door"), and when the narrator speaks of him (10:6), the pronouns for Jesus take the usual span.

decisions.choice: opens the door (B); opens it (R); calls each of his own sheep by name (B, R)
decisions.reason: Balanced and Readable say what is opened; Readable also describes the doorkeeper's work instead of using the title. "Each" brings out that the Greek phrase means name by name.

records.greek: ὅταν τὰ ἴδια πάντα ἐκβάλῃ, ἔμπροσθεν αὐτῶν πορεύεται, καὶ τὰ πρόβατα αὐτῷ ἀκολουθεῖ, ὅτι οἴδασιν τὴν φωνὴν αὐτοῦ·
records.gloss: When the own all he puts out, ahead of them he goes, and the sheep him follow, because they know the voice of him;

L.4: When he has put out all his own, he goes ahead of them, and the sheep follow him, because they know his voice.

R.4: When all his own sheep are out, he walks in front of them. The sheep follow him, because they know his voice.

decisions.choice: put out: bring out, with the sense of getting every one of them out
decisions.reason: The verb often means to throw or drive out, and it is the word used in 9:34-35 when the Pharisees threw the healed man out. Here the shepherd puts his own sheep out of the fold; what the authorities did to the man in hostility, the shepherd does for his flock's good. The force here is not violence but making sure that all his own are out.

decisions.choice: the shepherd walks in front and the sheep follow
alternatives: the shepherd drives the flock from behind
decisions.reason: Shepherds in the land of Israel led their flocks from the front, calling to them, and the sheep followed the voice they knew. The picture of a shepherd going before his flock is used of God (Psalm 80:2; Isaiah 40:11).

decisions.choice: because they know his voice: knowing his voice is the reason they follow
decisions.reason: The sheep do not follow because they are forced but because they recognise the one who calls them, which prepares for 10:14 ("I know my own and my own know me").

decisions.choice: all his own sheep; brought ... out (B, R)
decisions.reason: The Greek says "all his own"; Balanced and Readable supply "sheep", which the context makes clear, and use the gentler "brought out" for the verb (meaning decision m1).

records.greek: ἀλλοτρίῳ δὲ οὐ μὴ ἀκολουθήσουσιν ἀλλὰ φεύξονται ἀπ’ αὐτοῦ, ὅτι οὐκ οἴδασι τῶν ἀλλοτρίων τὴν φωνήν.
records.gloss: A stranger but not not they will follow but they will flee from him, because not they know of the strangers the voice.

L.5: But a stranger they will by no means follow, but they will flee from him, because they do not know the voice of strangers."

R.5: But they will never go after a stranger. They will run away from him, because they do not know a stranger's voice."

decisions.choice: a strong denial: they will certainly not follow
alternatives: a simple future: they will not follow
decisions.reason: The Greek puts two negatives together, the strongest way to deny something in the future.

decisions.choice: stranger: someone who does not belong to them
decisions.reason: The word means someone who belongs to another, not to this flock. It is not a foreigner by nation but a voice the sheep do not recognise as their shepherd's.

decisions.choice: the picture fits the man in chapter 9: he would not follow the Pharisees but listened to Jesus
alternatives: no connection with the preceding story
decisions.reason: The man born blind refused to be led by the Pharisees who questioned him (9:27-33), was thrown out (9:34), and then heard Jesus and worshiped him (9:35-38). The picture describes what has just happened, though Jesus does not name him.

decisions.choice: not ... at all (B); never (R); run (away)
decisions.reason: Plain words for the strong denial (meaning decision m1) and for fleeing.

records.greek: ταύτην τὴν παροιμίαν εἶπεν αὐτοῖς ὁ Ἰησοῦς· ἐκεῖνοι δὲ οὐκ ἔγνωσαν τίνα ἦν ἃ ἐλάλει αὐτοῖς.
records.gloss: This the figure said to them the Jesus; those but not understood what were [the things] which he was speaking to them.

L.6: Jesus told them this figure of speech, but they did not understand what the things were that He was saying to them.

R.6: Jesus used this picture to teach them, but they did not understand what He meant.

decisions.choice: a figure of speech: a saying with a hidden meaning that has to be worked out
alternatives: a parable in the sense of the stories in the other Gospels
decisions.reason: This is not the word the other Gospels use for Jesus's parables. It means a veiled or figurative saying, and in the Greek Old Testament it is used for proverbs. John uses it again when Jesus promises that he will no longer speak in figures but plainly (16:25, 29). Here it describes the picture of 10:1-5, whose meaning Jesus has not yet given.

decisions.choice: them: the Pharisees of 9:40-41
decisions.reason: The emphatic "those" points back to the people Jesus has been speaking to, the Pharisees who said, "We are not blind too, are we?" (9:40). Those who claim to see do not understand.

decisions.choice: they did not understand what his words meant
alternatives: they did not hear what he said
decisions.reason: They heard the words but did not grasp what they referred to, as often in John (8:27; 12:16). This is why Jesus goes on to explain (10:7).

decisions.choice: figure of speech (L, B); picture (R)
decisions.reason: "Parable" would bring in the word of the other Gospels, which John does not use (meaning decision m1). Readable uses a plain word for the same thing.

decisions.choice: Jesus told them (L); Jesus spoke ... to them (B)
alternatives: This figure of speech Jesus told them
decisions.reason: The Greek puts "this figure" first for emphasis; English puts the subject first, and Literal follows English order here because the fronted object reads awkwardly.

records.greek: Εἶπεν οὖν πάλιν αὐτοῖς ὁ Ἰησοῦς· Ἀμὴν ἀμὴν λέγω ὑμῖν ὅτι ἐγώ εἰμι ἡ θύρα τῶν προβάτων.
records.gloss: Said therefore again to them the Jesus, "Truly truly I say to you that I am the door of the sheep.

L.7: So Jesus said again to them, "Truly, truly I say to you, I am the door of the sheep.

R.7: So Jesus spoke to them again. "I tell you the truth: I am the door for the sheep.

decisions.choice: the door of the sheep (SBLGNT)
alternatives: the shepherd of the sheep (one early papyrus, P75, and some Coptic witnesses)
decisions.reason: Almost all manuscripts read "the door". A few early witnesses, the papyrus P75 among them, read "the shepherd", which is probably a change to fit 10:11. "The door" is the harder reading and is supported by 10:9. A footnote gives the other reading. A reviewer should check this against the apparatus.

decisions.choice: the door for the sheep: the door by which the sheep go in and out
alternatives: the door to the sheep, by which shepherds come to them
decisions.reason: In verses 1-2 the door is the way the shepherd comes to the sheep; in verse 9 it is the way the sheep go in and out. Jesus is the second here, as verse 9 makes plain, but the first is not excluded: those who came another way (verse 8) did not come through him.

decisions.choice: I am with a predicate: one of the sayings in which Jesus says who he is
alternatives: an echo of the divine name
decisions.reason: With a predicate the words are ordinary grammar. It is one of a series of such sayings (6:35; 8:12; 10:9, 11; 11:25; 14:6; 15:1), in which Jesus takes a picture and says that he is what it points to.

decisions.choice: so ... again: because they did not understand, he speaks again and explains
decisions.reason: The connecting word ties this to 10:6: Jesus explains the figure, taking up its parts one by one, first the door and then (10:11) the shepherd.

decisions.choice: the door of the sheep (L); the door for the sheep (B, R)
decisions.reason: Balanced and Readable show which door is meant (meaning decision m2). "Door" is kept at every level, as in 10:1-2.

records.greek: πάντες ὅσοι ἦλθον πρὸ ἐμοῦ κλέπται εἰσὶν καὶ λῃσταί· ἀλλ’ οὐκ ἤκουσαν αὐτῶν τὰ πρόβατα.
records.gloss: All as many as came before me thieves are and bandits; but not heard them the sheep.

L.8: All who came before Me are thieves and bandits; but the sheep did not hear them.

R.8: All who came before Me, claiming to be shepherds, are thieves and bandits. But the sheep did not listen to them.

decisions.choice: all who came before me: those who came claiming to lead God's people in his place, not Moses and the prophets
alternatives: every teacher and prophet before Jesus
only the Pharisees of his own day
decisions.reason: Jesus speaks of the prophets with respect: Moses wrote about him (5:46), Abraham rejoiced to see his day (8:56), and Isaiah saw his glory (12:41). The ones meant are those who came to the flock by another way, as in verse 1: leaders who used the people for themselves, like the shepherds of Ezekiel 34, and men who claimed to be the deliverer and led people into ruin. The present tense "are" may point especially to leaders still at work, such as those who had just thrown out the healed man. Who exactly is meant is not stated.

decisions.choice: before me (SBLGNT)
alternatives: the words left out (some early manuscripts)
decisions.reason: Some early witnesses leave out "before me", probably to avoid the impression that Jesus condemned the prophets; without them the sentence reads "All who came are thieves and bandits". The SBLGNT keeps the words. A reviewer should check the evidence against the apparatus.

decisions.choice: did not hear them: did not listen to them or follow them
alternatives: did not hear the sound of their voices
decisions.reason: As in verse 3, hearing means responding. The true sheep did not follow them, as the sheep in verse 5 flee from a stranger.

decisions.choice: claiming to be shepherds
decisions.reason: Readable makes explicit who "came": not everyone who lived earlier, but those who came to the flock as leaders (meaning decision m1). This goes beyond what the Greek says and reflects the uncertain decision m1.

decisions.choice: before {{deity_pronoun:me|Me}}
decisions.reason: From here Jesus applies the picture to himself, so "me" takes the deity_pronoun span (see 10:3).

records.greek: ἐγώ εἰμι ἡ θύρα· δι’ ἐμοῦ ἐάν τις εἰσέλθῃ σωθήσεται καὶ εἰσελεύσεται καὶ ἐξελεύσεται καὶ νομὴν εὑρήσει.
records.gloss: I am the door; through me if anyone enters he will be saved and will go in and will go out and pasture will find.

L.9: I am the door; through Me, if anyone enters, they will be saved, and will go in and will go out and will find pasture.

R.9: I am the door. If anyone comes in through Me, they will be saved. They will go in and out, and will find good grass to eat.

decisions.choice: will be saved: kept safe and given life, as a sheep in the fold and as a person who comes to Jesus
decisions.reason: In the picture the sheep that comes in by the door is safe from thieves. Applied to people, being saved in John means being rescued from perishing and given eternal life (3:16-17; 5:34; 12:47). Both are in view.

decisions.choice: go in and go out: live freely and safely
decisions.reason: Going in and going out is a Hebrew way of speaking of the whole of a person's life and daily movement (Deuteronomy 28:6; Psalm 121:8). Moses asked for a leader who would go out and come in before the people, so that they would not be like sheep without a shepherd (Numbers 27:17).

decisions.choice: find pasture: the shepherd's provision, as in Psalm 23 and Ezekiel 34
decisions.reason: God leads his flock to green pastures (Psalm 23:2) and promises to feed his sheep in good pasture on the mountains of Israel (Ezekiel 34:14).

decisions.choice: through me: placed first for emphasis
decisions.reason: The Greek puts "through me" before "if anyone enters": it is through him, and no other way (verse 1), that anyone comes in.

decisions.choice: anyone ... {{gender:they|he}}
decisions.reason: "Anyone" means any person, man or woman; the following pronoun takes the gender setting, with "he" as the alternative.

decisions.choice: good grass to eat
decisions.reason: Readable says what pasture is for sheep, a place to graze.

records.greek: ὁ κλέπτης οὐκ ἔρχεται εἰ μὴ ἵνα κλέψῃ καὶ θύσῃ καὶ ἀπολέσῃ· ἐγὼ ἦλθον ἵνα ζωὴν ἔχωσιν καὶ περισσὸν ἔχωσιν.
records.gloss: The thief not comes except that he may steal and slaughter and destroy; I came that life they may have and abundance they may have.

L.10: The thief does not come except to steal and slaughter and destroy; I came that they may have life and may have [it] beyond measure.

R.10: A thief has only one reason for coming: to steal the sheep, kill them and destroy them. But I came so that they can have life, life that overflows.

decisions.choice: slaughter: kill as an animal is killed for its meat
decisions.reason: The verb is used of killing animals, often in sacrifice, and of slaughtering for food (Luke 15:23). In a picture of sheep the sense is butchering; there is no thought of sacrifice here.

decisions.choice: destroy and life: perishing and eternal life
alternatives: physical harm and physical life only
decisions.reason: The verb "destroy" is the one John uses for perishing (3:16; 10:28), and the life Jesus gives is eternal life, which begins now (3:15-16; 5:24; 10:28). The thief brings the sheep to ruin; Jesus came to give them life that does not end.

decisions.choice: more than enough: life in full measure, beyond what is needed
decisions.reason: The word means what goes beyond the measure, an overflowing amount. It describes the fullness of the life Jesus gives, not wealth or comfort. The contrast is with shepherds who fed themselves instead of the flock (Ezekiel 34:2-3).

decisions.choice: the thief comes only to ...; I came that ...: two comings set against each other
decisions.reason: The construction "not ... except" limits the thief's purpose to harm. Jesus's "I came" answers it and recalls "all who came before me" (verse 8).

decisions.choice: beyond measure (L); in overflowing measure (B); life that overflows (R)
decisions.reason: These words say what the Greek word says, an amount that goes past the measure (meaning decision m3), without the wording familiar from other versions. Literal brackets "it", which the Greek leaves understood.

decisions.choice: to steal the sheep, kill them and destroy them
alternatives: to steal and kill and destroy
decisions.reason: Readable supplies the sheep as the object, which the picture implies.

records.greek: Ἐγώ εἰμι ὁ ποιμὴν ὁ καλός· ὁ ποιμὴν ὁ καλὸς τὴν ψυχὴν αὐτοῦ τίθησιν ὑπὲρ τῶν προβάτων·
records.gloss: I am the shepherd the good; the shepherd the good the life of him lays down for the sheep;

L.11: I am the good shepherd. The good shepherd lays down His life for the sheep.

R.11: I am the good shepherd. The good shepherd gives up His life for the sheep.

decisions.choice: good: the true and worthy shepherd, the model of what a shepherd should be
alternatives: morally good as opposed to wicked
decisions.reason: The word (καλός) is not the usual word for moral goodness. It describes what is fine, worthy and as it should be: the shepherd who is everything a shepherd ought to be, set against the thieves and robbers of 10:1, 8, 10 and the hired man of verse 12. It also carries a note of what is admirable, as in 2:10 (the good wine). Its proof is given at once: he lays down his life for the sheep. The Greek puts the article twice, "the shepherd, the good one", which marks him out as the one true shepherd, not one good shepherd among others.

decisions.choice: I am the good shepherd: Jesus claims the shepherd role that the Scriptures give to God and to his promised king
alternatives: only a picture drawn from daily life
decisions.reason: In the Scriptures God is the shepherd of his people (Psalm 23:1; 80:2; Isaiah 40:11). In Ezekiel 34 God condemns the shepherds of Israel who fed themselves and let the flock be scattered, and promises to seek and rescue his sheep himself (34:11-16) and to set over them one shepherd, his servant David (34:23). After the leaders have thrown out the man born blind (9:34), Jesus presents himself as that shepherd. This is one of the "I am" sayings with a predicate (6:35; 8:12; 10:7, 9; 11:25; 14:6; 15:1); the stressed "I" sets him against all false shepherds.

decisions.choice: lays down his life: gives up his life of his own will, by dying
decisions.reason: To lay down one's life (τίθημι with ψυχή) is a way of speaking that John uses again and again: 10:15, 17-18; 13:37-38; 15:13; 1 John 3:16. It means giving up one's life in death, freely. Verses 17-18 make clear that Jesus means his own death, which he gives of his own accord. A shepherd in Israel might risk his life against wild animals (1 Samuel 17:34-35); this shepherd goes further and dies for the flock. Here ψυχή means life itself, not the soul as one part of a person.

decisions.choice: for: on behalf of, for the good of the sheep
alternatives: in the place of the sheep
decisions.reason: The preposition (ὑπέρ) means "on behalf of": the shepherd dies so that the sheep may live. John uses it of Jesus's death in 6:51 (for the life of the world), 11:50-52 (one man dying for the people) and 15:13. In 11:50 the thought of one dying instead of many is near, but the word itself says that the death is for their benefit.

decisions.choice: the good shepherd (every level)
decisions.reason: "Good" in its older, fuller sense of worthy and true covers what the Greek word means (meaning decision m1), and "the good shepherd" is the name by which this saying is known. The Greek leaves little room for other wording, so this sentence is close to other translations; it is not taken from them. Other words for the adjective each catch only part of its sense.

decisions.choice: his: deity_pronoun setting
alternatives: his, with no setting, as for a figure in a picture
decisions.reason: The second half reads like a general saying about any good shepherd, but Jesus has just said that he is the good shepherd, and the saying describes his own death (verses 15, 17-18). The pronoun therefore refers to him and takes the deity_pronoun setting, unlike the shepherd of 10:2-4, a figure in a picture whom Jesus has not yet named as himself.

decisions.choice: gives up his life
decisions.reason: Readable uses an everyday phrase for the idiom (meaning decision m3) that keeps the sense of a life given freely.

records.heading: The good shepherd

records.greek: ὁ μισθωτὸς καὶ οὐκ ὢν ποιμήν, οὗ οὐκ ἔστιν τὰ πρόβατα ἴδια, θεωρεῖ τὸν λύκον ἐρχόμενον καὶ ἀφίησιν τὰ πρόβατα καὶ φεύγει καὶ ὁ λύκος ἁρπάζει αὐτὰ καὶ σκορπίζει ὅτι μισθωτός ἐστιν καὶ οὐ μέλει αὐτῷ περὶ τῶν προβάτων.
records.gloss: The hired man and not being shepherd, whose not are the sheep own, sees the wolf coming and leaves the sheep and flees, and the wolf snatches them and scatters, \v 13 because a hired man he is and not [it] is a care to him about the sheep.

L.12: The hired man, who is not a shepherd, whose own the sheep are not, sees the wolf coming and leaves the sheep and flees, and the wolf snatches them and scatters [them],
L.13: because he is a hired man and the sheep are no concern to him.

R.12: A worker hired for pay is not a shepherd, and the sheep do not belong to him. When he sees a wolf coming, he leaves the sheep and gets away. Then the wolf grabs the sheep and chases them in all directions.
R.13: The man gets away because he is only working for the money. He does not really care about the sheep.

decisions.choice: the hired man: a worker paid to watch the flock, who has no stake in it
decisions.reason: Flocks were often kept by the owner or his family (Genesis 29:9; 1 Samuel 16:11), but hired men were also used. A man paid by the day stood to lose nothing of his own if the flock was lost. The contrast is drawn twice: he is not a shepherd, and the sheep are not his own. The good shepherd, by contrast, calls the sheep "my own" (verse 14; compare 10:3-4).

decisions.choice: and not being a shepherd: "and" adds a description of the same man
alternatives: the hired man and someone else who is not a shepherd
decisions.reason: Only one person is meant. The little word "and" joins a second description to the first: the hired man, who is also no shepherd. Verse 13 speaks of him alone.

decisions.choice: the wolf that snatches and scatters: the danger the flock faces when its keepers fail
alternatives: a particular enemy Jesus has in mind
decisions.reason: In the Scriptures the people of God are scattered and become prey for wild animals when their shepherds care only for themselves (Ezekiel 34:5-8; Zechariah 11:16-17; compare Jeremiah 23:1-2). The wolf is part of the picture; Jesus does not say whom it stands for. Scattering the flock is undone by the shepherd who gathers (verse 16; 11:52).

decisions.choice: the sheep are no concern to him: he does not care what happens to them
decisions.reason: The phrase (μέλει) means "it matters to someone"; with "not" it means that he has no concern for them. It explains why he runs: his care is for his pay, not for the flock. In the setting of chapter 9, the picture stands against leaders who cast out one of the flock (9:34), though Jesus does not name the hired man.

decisions.choice: He flees because (B); The man gets away because (R); works only for pay, working for the money
alternatives: because he is a hired man (Literal)
decisions.reason: Balanced and Readable begin verse 13 as a new sentence, so they repeat the verb it explains, and they spell out what being a hired man means (meaning decision m1).

decisions.choice: seizes them and scatters the flock (B); grabs the sheep and chases them in all directions (R)
decisions.reason: The Greek gives "them" once for both verbs; Balanced and Readable supply an object for the second.

records.greek: ἐγώ εἰμι ὁ ποιμὴν ὁ καλός, καὶ γινώσκω τὰ ἐμὰ καὶ γινώσκουσί με τὰ ἐμά, καθὼς γινώσκει με ὁ πατὴρ κἀγὼ γινώσκω τὸν πατέρα, καὶ τὴν ψυχήν μου τίθημι ὑπὲρ τῶν προβάτων.
records.gloss: I am the shepherd the good, and I know the mine and know me the mine, \v 15 just as knows me the Father and-I know the Father, and the life of me I lay down for the sheep.

L.14: I am the good shepherd, and I know those [that are] Mine, and those [that are] Mine know Me,
L.15: just as the Father knows Me and I know the Father; and I lay down My life for the sheep.

R.14: I am the good shepherd. I know My sheep, and they know Me.
R.15: It is the same as the way the Father knows Me and I know Him. And I give up My life for the sheep.

decisions.choice: know: a personal knowing that belongs to a relationship
decisions.reason: The shepherd knows each sheep, and they know him, as in 10:3-4 where he calls them by name and they know his voice. In the Scriptures to know someone often means to be bound to them in care and loyalty (Exodus 33:12; Jeremiah 1:5; Amos 3:2). Knowing God in this way is eternal life (17:3).

decisions.choice: just as: the knowing between Jesus and his sheep is like the knowing between the Father and the Son, and comes from it
alternatives: a new sentence beginning with verse 15
decisions.reason: The word (καθώς) both compares and grounds, as often in John (15:9-10; 17:18, 21). The bond between the shepherd and the sheep has its pattern and source in the bond between the Father and the Son. The SBLGNT punctuation joins verse 15 to verse 14 as one sentence.

decisions.choice: mine: the sheep who belong to him
decisions.reason: The Greek has a neuter plural, "the mine", to match "sheep". The sheep belong to the shepherd, unlike those of the hired man (verse 12); in 17:6 Jesus says that those the Father gave him were the Father's, and he gave them to Jesus.

decisions.choice: and mine know me (SBLGNT)
alternatives: "and I am known by mine" (many later manuscripts)
decisions.reason: The older manuscripts have the active "mine know me", which matches the pairing in verse 15 (the Father knows me, I know the Father). Many later manuscripts have the passive "I am known by mine". The sense is close either way. A reviewer should check this against the apparatus.

decisions.choice: those [that are] mine (L); those who are mine (B)
decisions.reason: Literal and Balanced keep the repeated phrase without naming the sheep, as the Greek does (meaning decision m3). Readable says "my sheep" and then "they".

decisions.choice: It is the same as the way
decisions.reason: Readable makes verse 15 its own sentence and shows the comparison plainly (meaning decision m2). It uses "gives up my life", as in verse 11.

records.greek: καὶ ἄλλα πρόβατα ἔχω ἃ οὐκ ἔστιν ἐκ τῆς αὐλῆς ταύτης· κἀκεῖνα δεῖ με ἀγαγεῖν, καὶ τῆς φωνῆς μου ἀκούσουσιν, καὶ γενήσονται μία ποίμνη, εἷς ποιμήν.
records.gloss: And other sheep I have which not are from the fold this; and-those it is necessary me to bring, and the voice of me they will hear, and they will become one flock, one shepherd.

L.16: And I have other sheep, which are not of this fold; those also I must bring, and they will listen to My voice, and they will become one flock, one shepherd.

R.16: I have other sheep too. They are not in this sheep pen. I must bring them also. They will listen to My voice. Then they will all be one flock, with one shepherd.

decisions.choice: other sheep: people outside Israel, the Gentiles, who will come to belong to Jesus
decisions.reason: Jesus does not say who they are. In 11:51-52 John explains that Jesus would die not for the nation only but to gather into one the scattered children of God, and in 12:20-32 the coming of Greeks to see Jesus leads him to speak of drawing all people to himself. The Gentiles are the most likely meaning. The words could also mean Jews scattered among the nations (compare 7:35), and the text does not settle it.

decisions.choice: fold and flock: two different words, the enclosure and the flock itself
decisions.reason: The first word (αὐλή) is the walled yard where sheep were kept at night, the word used in 10:1. The second (ποίμνη) is the flock, the sheep themselves. Jesus does not say that the other sheep will be brought into this fold, but that the sheep from both places will form one flock. Their unity lies in the one shepherd whose voice they hear, not in one enclosure.

decisions.choice: I must: the necessity of God's purpose
alternatives: a duty he has taken on himself
decisions.reason: The word (δεῖ) is used in John for what God's plan requires (3:14, 30; 4:4; 9:4; 12:34; 20:9). The bringing of the other sheep is part of what the Father has given the Son to do.

decisions.choice: one flock, one shepherd: God's promise of a reunited people under one shepherd
decisions.reason: Ezekiel promises that God will set over his flock "one shepherd, my servant David" (Ezekiel 34:23), and that the divided kingdoms will become one nation with one shepherd over them all (Ezekiel 37:22, 24). Jesus takes up the promise and widens it to take in the other sheep. Compare his prayer that those who believe may be one (17:20-23).

decisions.choice: they will become (SBLGNT, plural)
decisions.reason: Some manuscripts have the singular verb, so that the sentence reads "there will be one flock". The SBLGNT has the plural, with the sheep as its subject: they will become one flock. The sense is the same. A reviewer should check the evidence against the apparatus.

decisions.choice: fold (L, B); sheep pen (R); flock (every level)
decisions.reason: Two different words are kept apart (meaning decision m2), so that the reader can see that the unity is a flock under one shepherd, not one enclosure. Readable uses "sheep pen", a plainer word for the enclosure.

decisions.choice: listen to
decisions.reason: With this construction the verb means to hear and heed, as the sheep do in 10:3, 27; "listen to" keeps both.

records.greek: διὰ τοῦτό με ὁ πατὴρ ἀγαπᾷ ὅτι ἐγὼ τίθημι τὴν ψυχήν μου, ἵνα πάλιν λάβω αὐτήν.
records.gloss: Because of this me the Father loves, that I lay down the life of me, so that again I may take it.

L.17: For this [reason] the Father loves Me, because I lay down My life, so that I may take it again.

R.17: The Father loves Me because I give up My life. I give it up so that I can take it back again.

decisions.choice: for this reason ... because: "this" points forward to the clause that follows
decisions.reason: John often uses "for this reason" followed by "because" to state a reason and then spell it out (5:16, 18; 8:47; 12:18, 39). Here the reason is that Jesus lays down his life. What he has said in verses 11-16 is gathered into it.

decisions.choice: the Father loves the Son in his self-giving, which is one with the Father's own will
alternatives: the Son earns the Father's love by dying
decisions.reason: The Father has loved the Son before the world was made (17:24; compare 3:35; 5:20). Jesus's free giving of his life is his perfect obedience to the Father (verse 18; 14:31), and in it the Father's love for him is shown and answered (15:10). The verse does not say that the love began with the death.

decisions.choice: so that I may take it again: his death has its rising in view
alternatives: "with the result that", without a purpose
decisions.reason: The word (ἵνα) states the purpose. Jesus lays down his life not to be lost in death but in order to take it again. The cross and the resurrection are one act of obedience.

decisions.choice: take it again: Jesus will take back his life in the resurrection
alternatives: receive it back from the Father, as a gift only
decisions.reason: The verb (λαμβάνω) can mean "take" or "receive". Jesus speaks of raising up the temple of his body (2:19-21), as here of taking up his life. Elsewhere the New Testament says that God raised him (Acts 2:24; Romans 10:9). The two belong together: verse 18 says that the Father gave him authority to take it again.

decisions.choice: This is why ...: because (B); The Father loves me because (R)
decisions.reason: Balanced keeps both halves of the Greek pattern with a colon, so that "this" points forward (meaning decision m1); Readable gives the reason once.

decisions.choice: take it up again (B); take it back again (R)
decisions.reason: "Take it up" and "take it back" make plain that he will have his life again (meaning decision m4). Readable says "give up" for "lay down", as in verse 11.

records.greek: οὐδεὶς αἴρει αὐτὴν ἀπ’ ἐμοῦ, ἀλλ’ ἐγὼ τίθημι αὐτὴν ἀπ’ ἐμαυτοῦ.
records.gloss: No one takes it from me, but I lay down it from myself.

L.18: No one takes it from Me, but I lay it down of Myself.

R.18: No one takes My life from Me. I give it up because I choose to.

decisions.choice: takes (SBLGNT, present tense)
alternatives: "took" (some early manuscripts, among them P45 and Codex Vaticanus, and the first hand of Codex Sinaiticus)
decisions.reason: A few early manuscripts have the past tense: no one took it from me. That reading looks back on the death as a past event. The SBLGNT has the present, which fits the present "I lay it down" in the same sentence. A reviewer should check this against the apparatus.

decisions.choice: of myself: by my own free choice
alternatives: on my own authority, apart from the Father
decisions.reason: Elsewhere Jesus says that he does nothing "of himself", that is, apart from the Father (5:19, 30; 7:28; 8:28, 42). Here the phrase answers "no one takes it from me": he is not forced. The next sentence shows that this free choice is also the Father's command; the two are not in conflict.

decisions.choice: no one takes it: even in his death Jesus is not a victim of others' power
decisions.reason: Others will seek to kill him (5:18; 7:1; 8:59), and he will be put to death, but John shows him in control: no one could seize him before his hour (7:30; 8:20), he tells Pilate that Pilate's power is given from above (19:11), and at the end he hands over his spirit (19:30).

decisions.choice: of my own accord (B); because I choose to (R)
decisions.reason: Balanced and Readable give the sense of free choice (meaning decision m2), which "of myself" might hide. Readable names "my life" in place of "it".

records.greek: ἐξουσίαν ἔχω θεῖναι αὐτήν, καὶ ἐξουσίαν ἔχω πάλιν λαβεῖν αὐτήν· ταύτην τὴν ἐντολὴν ἔλαβον παρὰ τοῦ πατρός μου.
records.gloss: Authority I have to lay down it, and authority I have again to take it; this the command I received from the Father of me.

L.18: I have authority to lay it down, and I have authority to take it again; this command I received from My Father."

R.18: I have the right to give it up, and I have the right to take it back again. This is what My Father has commanded Me."

decisions.choice: authority: the right, given to him, and the power to act on it
decisions.reason: The word (ἐξουσία) means a right to act that has been granted, together with the power to carry it out. The Father has given the Son authority to judge (5:27) and authority over all people (17:2). Pilate will claim authority over Jesus's life (19:10), and Jesus will answer that Pilate would have none unless it were given him from above (19:11).

decisions.choice: command: the charge the Father has given the Son
decisions.reason: In John the Father's command to the Son is the whole task he was sent to do and the words he is to speak (12:49-50; 14:31). "This command" covers both laying down his life and taking it again.

decisions.choice: the right ... This is what my Father has commanded me
alternatives: authority ... This command I received (Literal, Balanced)
decisions.reason: Readable uses an everyday word for the authority he has been given (meaning decision m1) and turns the noun "command" into a verb.

records.greek: Σχίσμα πάλιν ἐγένετο ἐν τοῖς Ἰουδαίοις διὰ τοὺς λόγους τούτους.
records.gloss: A division again came to be among the Jews because of the words these.

L.19: Again a division came about among the Jews because of these words.

R.19: Once again the Jews who were listening did not agree with each other about what Jesus said.

decisions.choice: the Jews: the people who heard Jesus speak, among them some of the Pharisees (9:40)
alternatives: the Jewish people as a whole
decisions.reason: Jesus has been speaking to those around him after the healing of the man born blind, among them Pharisees (9:40-41). These hearers are divided: some are hostile, some are open to him (verse 21). So the word does not here mean a united group of authorities hostile to Jesus, and it does not mean the people as a whole: Jesus himself is a Jew (4:9, 22), and so are his disciples.

decisions.choice: division again: the hearers split into opposing sides, as before
decisions.reason: The word (σχίσμα) means a split or rift. John has already told of the crowd divided over Jesus (7:43) and the Pharisees divided over the healing (9:16). "Again" points back to these. Jesus's coming divides those who meet him (compare 9:39).

decisions.choice: these words: what Jesus said in 10:1-18
alternatives: only the last words about his death
decisions.reason: The division is over all he has said about the shepherd and the sheep, ending with his words about laying down his life and taking it again.

decisions.choice: the Jews who were listening (B, R)
decisions.reason: Here the word means the hearers in this scene (meaning decision m1), who are divided, not the authorities as one body. Balanced and Readable keep the word John wrote and tie it to the people present, so that no reader takes it to mean every Jew.

decisions.choice: were divided (B); did not agree with each other (R)
decisions.reason: Balanced and Readable turn the noun into a verb, and Readable names what the words were.

records.heading: Divided over Jesus

records.greek: ἔλεγον δὲ πολλοὶ ἐξ αὐτῶν· Δαιμόνιον ἔχει καὶ μαίνεται· τί αὐτοῦ ἀκούετε;
records.gloss: Were saying and many of them, "A demon he has and is raving; why him do you hear?"

L.20: And many of them were saying, "He has a demon and is raving mad; why do you listen to Him?"

R.20: Many of them said, "A demon has driven Him mad! Why do you listen to Him?"

decisions.choice: he has a demon and is raving: he is mad, in the grip of an evil spirit
alternatives: two separate charges, possession and madness
decisions.reason: Here the two charges stand side by side, and the second explains the first: to say someone "has a demon" was a way of calling him mad (7:20; 8:48, 52). The verb (μαίνομαι) means to rave, to be out of one's mind (Acts 12:15; 26:24-25). It is an insult rather than a diagnosis.

decisions.choice: were saying: the imperfect shows talk that went on among them
decisions.reason: The tense describes what many were saying, and others were saying in reply (verse 21). It pictures the argument among the hearers.

decisions.choice: why do you listen to him?: a question meant to stop others listening
alternatives: a real question asking for a reason
decisions.reason: The question is aimed at those who are still listening: there is no reason to give attention to a madman. The irony is that the sheep do listen to the shepherd's voice (verses 3, 16, 27).

decisions.choice: out of his mind (B); A demon has driven him mad (R)
decisions.reason: Balanced keeps both charges and gives the second in an everyday phrase. Readable joins them into one, as 8:48 does, showing that the demon is the cause of the madness (meaning decision m1). It keeps the demon, because verse 21 answers that very word.

records.greek: ἄλλοι ἔλεγον· Ταῦτα τὰ ῥήματα οὐκ ἔστιν δαιμονιζομένου· μὴ δαιμόνιον δύναται τυφλῶν ὀφθαλμοὺς ἀνοῖξαι;
records.gloss: Others were saying, "These the sayings not are of one demon-possessed; not a demon is able of blind [ones] eyes to open?"

L.21: Others were saying, "These are not the sayings of one who has a demon. A demon is not able to open [the] eyes of [the] blind, is it?"

R.21: Others said, "Someone who has a demon does not talk like this. And can a demon make blind people able to see? Of course not!"

decisions.choice: these sayings: what he says shows a sound mind, not a demon's raving
decisions.reason: They answer the charge of verse 20. The word (ῥῆμα) means things said; they find his words clear and full of sense, not the talk of a man possessed.

decisions.choice: can a demon open ...?: a question that expects the answer no
decisions.reason: The question begins with a word (μή) that expects "no". They do not merely deny the charge; they argue from the sign: giving sight is a work of God, not of a demon.

decisions.choice: open the eyes of the blind: the healing of the man born blind (chapter 9)
decisions.reason: The speakers point back to the sign of 9:1-7, and use the man's own argument (9:30-33): no one had ever opened the eyes of someone born blind, and only one from God could do it. The Scriptures speak of opening the eyes of the blind as God's work (Psalm 146:8; Isaiah 35:5; 42:7). As in 9:16, some draw the right conclusion from the sign.

decisions.choice: This is not how a man with a demon speaks (B); Someone who has a demon does not talk like this (R)
alternatives: These are not the sayings of one who has a demon (Literal)
decisions.reason: Balanced and Readable put the point in a natural English sentence. The speakers mean Jesus, a particular man, so Balanced says "a man".

decisions.choice: Surely ... cannot (B); Of course not! (R)
alternatives: A demon is not able ..., is it? (Literal)
decisions.reason: Each level shows that the question expects the answer no (meaning decision m2).

records.greek: Ἐγένετο τότε τὰ ἐγκαίνια ἐν τοῖς Ἱεροσολύμοις· χειμὼν ἦν, καὶ περιεπάτει ὁ Ἰησοῦς ἐν τῷ ἱερῷ ἐν τῇ στοᾷ τοῦ Σολομῶνος.
records.gloss: Took place then the Dedication in the Jerusalem; winter it was, \v 23 and was walking the Jesus in the temple in the colonnade of the Solomon.

L.22: At that time the [Feast of] Dedication took place in Jerusalem. It was winter,
L.23: and Jesus was walking in the temple, in the colonnade of Solomon.

R.22: Then it was time for the Feast of Dedication, also called Hanukkah, in Jerusalem. It was winter.
R.23: Jesus was walking in the temple area, along the covered walkway called Solomon's Colonnade.

decisions.choice: the Dedication: the festival remembering the rededication of the temple, known today as Hanukkah
decisions.reason: The word means a dedication or renewal. In 167 BC the Syrian king Antiochus IV set up pagan worship in the temple at Jerusalem. After Judas Maccabeus and his followers took the city back, they cleansed the temple and dedicated a new altar in December 164 BC, and decreed that the day be kept each year for eight days (1 Maccabees 4:36-59; 2 Maccabees 10:1-8). Unlike Passover and Tabernacles, it was not one of the festivals commanded in the Law of Moses. John names it as he names the other festivals (2:13; 7:2).

decisions.choice: it was winter: the festival fell in December
decisions.reason: The festival began on the twenty-fifth day of the month Kislev (1 Maccabees 4:52), which falls in December. The note dates the scene some two months after the Feast of Tabernacles of chapter 7, and it may explain why Jesus was in the covered colonnade rather than in the open courts. John does not say so, and no level adds it.

decisions.choice: the colonnade of Solomon: a roofed walkway on the east side of the temple courts
alternatives: a porch at the entrance of the sanctuary
decisions.reason: The word is used of a long colonnade: a row of columns carrying a roof, open on one side. Herod's temple courts were surrounded by colonnades, and the one along the east side was called Solomon's, after the builder of the first temple; the Jewish historian Josephus describes it. The first believers later met there (Acts 3:11; 5:12). It was a public place where teachers walked and talked with people.

decisions.choice: a festival of the temple's dedication as the setting for what Jesus says
decisions.reason: John sets these words at the feast that celebrated the consecration of the temple. Later in the same exchange Jesus speaks of himself as the one whom the Father consecrated and sent into the world (10:36), and earlier John has called his body a temple (2:19-21). The setting may be meant to bring these together, but John does not draw the link himself.

decisions.choice: temple courts (B); temple area (R)
decisions.reason: The word means the whole temple area, with its courts and colonnades, not the sanctuary itself (see the book's terms).

decisions.choice: also called Hanukkah; covered walkway
decisions.reason: Readable gives the festival the name most readers know today (meaning decision m1) and says what a colonnade is: a roofed walkway (meaning decision m3). "Hanukkah" is the Hebrew word for dedication, so the name adds nothing John does not say. Readable also breaks the record into short sentences.

records.greek: ἐκύκλωσαν οὖν αὐτὸν οἱ Ἰουδαῖοι καὶ ἔλεγον αὐτῷ· Ἕως πότε τὴν ψυχὴν ἡμῶν αἴρεις;
records.gloss: Surrounded therefore him the Jews and were saying to him, "Until when the soul of us you lift?

L.24: So the Jews surrounded Him and were saying to Him, "How long will You hold our soul in suspense?

R.24: The Jews who were there crowded around Him. They asked Him, "How long are You going to keep us guessing?

decisions.choice: the Jews: the hostile hearers who gathered around Jesus in the temple
alternatives: the Jewish people as a whole
decisions.reason: These questioners are hostile: Jesus tells them that they do not believe and are not his sheep (10:25-26), and in 10:31 and 10:39 they try to stone and to seize him for blasphemy, as had happened before (5:18; 8:59). Their demand sounds like the authorities' questions (1:19; 8:13), and leaders may well have been among them, but John does not single them out. The word names this group of hearers, not the people as a whole: Jesus, his disciples and the many who believe in him (10:42) are Jews.

decisions.choice: surrounded: they closed in around him
alternatives: gathered near him in a friendly way
decisions.reason: The verb means to encircle. It is used of armies surrounding a city (Luke 21:20). Here it pictures Jesus hemmed in by a group demanding an answer, in the colonnade where he was walking.

decisions.choice: how long will you keep us in suspense: their minds are held up, waiting for an answer
alternatives: how long will you trouble or annoy us
how long will you take away our life
decisions.reason: Word for word they say, "How long do you lift up our soul?" The phrase can mean to stir up someone's hopes or keep them hanging in uncertainty, and that fits the demand that follows, "tell us plainly" (10:24b). In later Greek a similar phrase can mean to vex or annoy someone, and the questioners may mean that too: they are impatient, not simply curious.

decisions.choice: the Jews who were there (B, R)
decisions.reason: Here the word means the group of hearers in the temple (meaning decision m1), not the authorities alone and not the Jewish people as a whole. Balanced and Readable keep the word John wrote, as 8:48 and 10:31 do, and tie it to the people present, so that no reader takes it to mean every Jew.

decisions.choice: {{deity_pronoun:he|He}}, {{deity_pronoun:him|Him}}, {{deity_pronoun:his|His}}, {{deity_pronoun:me|Me}}, {{deity_pronoun:my|My}}, {{deity_pronoun:mine|Mine}}, {{deity_pronoun:you|You}}
decisions.reason: Every pronoun for Christ or for God uses the deity_pronoun setting, including "me", "my" and "mine" when Jesus speaks of himself, and "you" when others speak to him. At the start of a sentence "He" or "My" is written plain. This applies throughout the passage.

decisions.choice: hold our soul in suspense (L); leave us in suspense (B); keep us guessing (R)
alternatives: lift up our soul (word for word)
decisions.reason: Word for word the phrase would suggest lifting up the soul in prayer, as in Psalm 25:1, which is not meant here. Literal keeps "soul" and supplies the sense of the idiom; Balanced and Readable say it in everyday words (meaning decision m3).

records.greek: εἰ σὺ εἶ ὁ χριστός, εἰπὲ ἡμῖν παρρησίᾳ.
records.gloss: If you are the Christ, tell us plainly."

L.24: If You are the Christ, tell us plainly."

R.24: If You are the Christ, tell us so clearly."

decisions.choice: the Christ: the Messiah, the anointed king God had promised
decisions.reason: With the article the word is a title, not a name: the one God would anoint to rule, whom the people expected (1:20, 41; 7:26-27, 41-42). The question is whether Jesus claims to be that person.

decisions.choice: plainly: in clear words, without figures of speech
decisions.reason: The word can mean speaking in public (7:26) or speaking plainly. Here it is the second: Jesus has been speaking in a figure about the shepherd and the sheep (10:6), and they want a direct yes or no. John uses the word the same way in 11:14 and 16:25, 29, where plain speech is set against figures.

decisions.choice: a demand for a direct claim that Jesus answers by pointing to his works
decisions.reason: In public Jesus has not called himself the Christ in so many words, though he has told the Samaritan woman (4:25-26) and the man born blind (9:35-37) who he is. A plain claim to be the Christ could be heard as a claim to be king, and could be used against him (compare 19:12). Jesus answers that he has already told them, and that his works speak for him (10:25).

decisions.choice: the {{christos:Christ|Messiah}}
decisions.reason: Where the Greek has "the Christ" as a title, every level writes "the" before the setting, so that the alternative reads "the Messiah" (see the book's terms).

decisions.choice: in plain words (B); clearly (R)
decisions.reason: "Openly" could suggest speaking in public; Balanced and Readable make clear that the questioners want direct speech (meaning decision m2). Readable adds "so" for the yes they want to hear.

records.greek: ἀπεκρίθη αὐτοῖς ὁ Ἰησοῦς· Εἶπον ὑμῖν καὶ οὐ πιστεύετε· τὰ ἔργα ἃ ἐγὼ ποιῶ ἐν τῷ ὀνόματι τοῦ πατρός μου ταῦτα μαρτυρεῖ περὶ ἐμοῦ·
records.gloss: Answered them the Jesus, "I told you, and not you believe; the works which I do in the name of the Father of me, these testify about me;

L.25: Jesus answered them, "I told you, and you do not believe. The works that I do in the name of My Father, these testify about Me.

R.25: Jesus answered, "I already told you, but you do not believe. The things I do with My Father's authority show you who I am.

decisions.choice: I told you: he has made his claim already, though not in the words they demand
alternatives: he had once said in so many words that he is the Christ
decisions.reason: John records no public saying in Jerusalem in which Jesus calls himself the Christ. But he has told them who he is in other words: that God is his own Father (5:17-18), that he is the light of the world (8:12), that before Abraham was, he is (8:58), and that he is the good shepherd (10:11-14). Their unbelief is not for lack of a clear word.

decisions.choice: the works: all that Jesus does, his signs above all
decisions.reason: John uses "works" for Jesus's deeds as the Father's own work done through him (5:17, 36; 9:3-4). They include the signs, such as the healing of the man born blind (9:1-7) that was still being argued about (10:21). Jesus points to them again in 10:32, 37-38 and 14:10-11.

decisions.choice: in the name of my Father: as his representative, with his authority
decisions.reason: To act in someone's name is to act for him, by his authority. Jesus has said that he came in his Father's name (5:43): his works are not his own project but the Father's.

decisions.choice: testify: the language of a witness in court
decisions.reason: John often uses the language of testimony, as in a trial. In 5:31-37 Jesus named the witnesses to him: John the Baptist, his works and the Father himself. The Law required more than one witness (Deuteronomy 19:15; compare 8:17-18). Here the works stand as witnesses in his case.

decisions.choice: are themselves witnesses for me (B); show you who I am, with my Father's authority (R)
decisions.reason: Balanced keeps the stress on "these" and the language of witness (meaning decision m4). Readable says what "in the name of" means (meaning decision m3) and what the testimony is about: who Jesus is, which is the question asked in 10:24.

records.greek: ἀλλὰ ὑμεῖς οὐ πιστεύετε, ὅτι οὐκ ἐστὲ ἐκ τῶν προβάτων τῶν ἐμῶν.
records.gloss: But you not believe, because not you are of the sheep the mine.

L.26: But you do not believe, because you are not of the sheep that are Mine.

R.26: But you do not believe, because you do not belong to My sheep.

decisions.choice: no further words after "my sheep" (SBLGNT)
alternatives: "... my sheep, as I said to you" (many later manuscripts)
decisions.reason: Many manuscripts, among them Codex Alexandrinus, Codex Bezae and most later ones, add "as I said to you" at the end of the verse, as the King James Version reflects. The words are not in the oldest papyri or in Codices Sinaiticus and Vaticanus. Jesus has not said these exact words before, so a scribe may have added them to point back to 10:14 and 10:16, or attached them to 10:27. A footnote gives the longer reading. A reviewer should check this against the apparatus.

decisions.choice: because you are not my sheep: belonging and believing go together
alternatives: they are not his sheep because they do not believe
decisions.reason: Jesus gives the reason for their unbelief: they do not belong to his flock. John says elsewhere that those the Father gives to Jesus come to him (6:37, 44, 65), and also that people are answerable for refusing to believe (3:18-19; 8:24; 9:41). The text holds both, as 6:37 does, without explaining how they fit.

decisions.choice: my sheep: the picture of the shepherd from 10:1-16
decisions.reason: Jesus takes up the picture he gave earlier: the sheep that know the shepherd's voice (10:3-4) and that he knows (10:14). The words "the sheep that are mine" stress belonging: they are his own.

decisions.choice: among my sheep (B); belong to my sheep (R)
alternatives: of the sheep that are mine (Literal)
decisions.reason: Plain English for being one of the flock that is his (meaning decision m3).

records.greek: τὰ πρόβατα τὰ ἐμὰ τῆς φωνῆς μου ἀκούουσιν, κἀγὼ γινώσκω αὐτά, καὶ ἀκολουθοῦσίν μοι, κἀγὼ δίδωμι αὐτοῖς ζωὴν αἰώνιον, καὶ οὐ μὴ ἀπόλωνται εἰς τὸν αἰῶνα, καὶ οὐχ ἁρπάσει τις αὐτὰ ἐκ τῆς χειρός μου.
records.gloss: The sheep the mine the voice of me hear, and I know them, and they follow me, \v 28 and I give to them life eternal, and not not they will perish into the age, and not will snatch anyone them out of the hand of me.

L.27: The sheep that are Mine hear My voice, and I know them, and they follow Me,
L.28: and I give them eternal life, and they will by no means perish, ever, and no one will snatch them out of My hand.

R.27: My sheep listen to My voice. I know them, and they follow Me.
R.28: I give them eternal life, the life of the age to come, which starts now. They will never be lost. No one will snatch them out of My hand.

decisions.choice: hear, know, follow: the marks of the sheep in 10:3-5 and 10:14
decisions.reason: Jesus repeats what he said in the picture of the shepherd: the sheep hear his voice and follow him (10:3-4), he knows his own (10:14), and they will not follow a stranger (10:5). Knowing here is personal, like the knowledge between the Father and the Son (10:15).

decisions.choice: they will never perish: a strong denial, for all time
decisions.reason: The Greek joins two negatives, the strongest way to deny that something will happen, and adds "to the age", which means for ever. Together they say that the sheep will not perish at any time. The verb is the one used in 3:16 and in 6:39, where Jesus says he will lose none of those the Father has given him.

decisions.choice: eternal life: a gift given now
decisions.reason: The verb is present: "I give". Eternal life is the life of the age to come, and in John it begins now for those who believe (3:36; 5:24; 6:47, 54).

decisions.choice: snatch out of my hand: take away by force from his keeping
decisions.reason: The verb is the one used of the wolf that snatches the sheep (10:12). The hand stands for power and protection, as often in Scripture (Deuteronomy 32:39; Isaiah 43:13). No one has the power to take the sheep from Jesus. The same words are used of the Father's hand in 10:29.

decisions.choice: The sheep that belong to me (B); My sheep (R); listen to (B, R)
decisions.reason: Literal and Balanced keep the stress that the Greek puts on "mine" by placing it after the noun; Readable uses the shorter "my". "Listen to" says that hearing here means heeding. Balanced and Readable break the long sentence and leave out the repeated "and".

decisions.choice: the life of the age to come, which starts now; be lost
decisions.reason: Readable explains "eternal life" once in the passage, as the book's terms allow (meaning decision m3). It says "be lost" for "perish", as it does in 3:16.

records.greek: ὁ πατήρ μου ὃ δέδωκέν μοι πάντων μεῖζων ἐστιν, καὶ οὐδεὶς δύναται ἁρπάζειν ἐκ τῆς χειρὸς τοῦ πατρός.
records.gloss: The Father of me, what he has given to me, than all greater is, and no one is able to snatch out of the hand of the Father.

L.29: My Father, as to what He has given Me, is greater than all, and no one is able to snatch [them] out of the hand of the Father.

R.29: My Father is the one who gave them to Me, and He is greater than anyone or anything. No one can snatch them out of the Father's hand.

decisions.choice: the SBLGNT reading: neuter "what" with masculine "greater" (ὃ ... μεῖζων)
alternatives: "What my Father has given me is greater than all": neuter "what" with neuter "greater" (Codex Vaticanus in its first hand, and Latin witnesses)
"My Father, who has given them to me, is greater than all": masculine "who" with masculine "greater" (papyrus 66, Codex Alexandrinus and most later manuscripts)
decisions.reason: The manuscripts differ in two small words: "what" or "who", and "greater" in the neuter or the masculine. The SBLGNT follows the mixed reading found in Codex Sinaiticus and a few others, neuter "what" with masculine "greater". Scribes had reason to smooth this harder reading into one of the easier ones, which favors it, but it is hard to construe (meaning decision m2). The reading with both words neuter makes the flock, the Father's gift, the thing that is greater than all; the reading with both masculine makes it the Father. A footnote gives the other readings. A reviewer should check the witnesses against the apparatus.

decisions.choice: the Father is greater than all; "what he has given me" stands loosely as the object of "has given"
alternatives: take "greater" as if it were neuter: what the Father has given me is greater than all
decisions.reason: In the SBLGNT text "greater" is masculine and agrees with "my Father", so the Father is the one who is greater than all. The neuter "what he has given me" is then a loose clause about the sheep, the Father's gift to Jesus, using the same neuter as in 6:37 and 6:39 for all the Father gives him. The sense is: my Father, who gave them to me, is greater than all. The other way of reading it, that the gift itself is greater than all, follows the variant rather than this text.

decisions.choice: no one can snatch them from the Father's hand: the sheep are kept by the Father as by the Son
decisions.reason: Verse 28 said that no one will snatch the sheep out of Jesus's hand; now it is the Father's hand. The reason is that the Father is greater than all, including any who would harm the flock (10:10, 12). The two hands hold the same sheep, which leads into 10:30.

decisions.choice: all: everyone and everything
decisions.reason: The form can be masculine or neuter, so it may mean all people or all things. No power of any kind is greater than the Father.

decisions.choice: as to what he has given me (L); who gave them to me (B, R); them (B, R)
alternatives: what he has given me is greater than all
who has given them to me
decisions.reason: Literal keeps the neuter "what" and shows by "as to" that the Father is the subject of "is greater" (meaning decision m2). Balanced and Readable say what the clause means: the Father gave the sheep to Jesus. The verb "snatch" has no object in Greek; the sheep are meant, so Literal brackets [them] and the other levels supply it.

records.greek: ἐγὼ καὶ ὁ πατὴρ ἕν ἐσμεν.
records.gloss: I and the Father one we are."

L.30: I and the Father are one."

R.30: The Father and I are one."

decisions.choice: one: neuter, "one thing", not "one person"
decisions.reason: The word for "one" (ἕν) is neuter. Jesus does not say that he and the Father are one and the same person: he says "we are", in the plural, and the two are named separately. The neuter speaks of a unity between two. John uses the same neuter when Jesus prays that his disciples may be one as he and the Father are one (17:11, 21-22).

decisions.choice: a unity of will and action, which the hearers took as a claim to be God
alternatives: a statement that the Father and the Son are the same person
decisions.reason: In context the unity is shown in what the two do: the same sheep are held in the Son's hand and the Father's hand (10:28-29), and Jesus does the Father's works (10:25, 37-38; 5:19). The hearers took the words as more than agreement: they picked up stones because, they said, "you, being a man, make yourself God" (10:31-33). John does not correct them on that point; he has said that the Word was God (1:1), and Jesus goes on to say that the Father is in him and he in the Father (10:38). The text states the unity without giving a later doctrinal formula for it.

decisions.choice: a possible echo of the confession that God is one
decisions.reason: Israel's confession says that the LORD our God is one (Deuteronomy 6:4). Placing Jesus within that oneness would explain why the hearers reacted as they did (10:31-33). But the words are not a quotation, and the echo may not be intended.

decisions.choice: The Father and I
decisions.reason: English usually names the other person first and "I" last. The Greek order puts "I" first; Literal keeps it. The meaning does not change.

records.greek: Ἐβάστασαν οὖν πάλιν λίθους οἱ Ἰουδαῖοι ἵνα λιθάσωσιν αὐτόν.
records.gloss: Took up therefore again stones the Jews that they might stone him.

L.31: So the Jews again picked up stones in order to stone Him.

R.31: Then the Jews standing around Jesus picked up stones again. They wanted to stone Him to death.

decisions.choice: the Jews: the hostile hearers who had gathered around Jesus in the temple at the feast of Dedication (10:24)
alternatives: the Jewish people as a whole
decisions.reason: They are the people who surrounded him in Solomon's colonnade and demanded that he say plainly whether he was the Christ (10:22-24). Their questions sound like those of the authorities (1:19; 8:13), and the leaders may well have been among them, but John does not single them out here. The word names this group of hearers, not the people as a whole: Jesus is himself a Jew (4:9, 22), and so are his disciples and, in 10:42, the many who believe in him.

decisions.choice: picked up stones to stone him: to put him to death on the spot for blasphemy
decisions.reason: Stoning was the law's penalty for blasphemy (Leviticus 24:16), and verse 33 names the charge. "Again" points back to 8:59, where they picked up stones after he said "before Abraham was, I am". Here they react to "I and the Father are one" (10:30). There is no trial; they mean to act at once.

decisions.choice: picked up: lifted, or perhaps went and got
decisions.reason: The verb usually means to lift and carry. It may mean that they had to fetch stones, but John's point is the same either way: they were ready to kill him.

decisions.choice: the Jews who had gathered around him (B); the Jews standing around Jesus (R)
decisions.reason: Here the word means the group of hearers of 10:24 (meaning decision m1), not the authorities alone and not the Jewish people as a whole. Balanced and Readable keep the word John wrote, as 8:48 does, and tie it to the people present, so that no reader takes it to mean every Jew.

decisions.choice: They wanted to stone him to death
decisions.reason: Readable breaks the sentence and says plainly that stoning was meant to kill (meaning decision m2).

records.heading: The charge of blasphemy

records.greek: ἀπεκρίθη αὐτοῖς ὁ Ἰησοῦς· Πολλὰ ἔργα καλὰ ἔδειξα ὑμῖν ἐκ τοῦ πατρός· διὰ ποῖον αὐτῶν ἔργον ἐμὲ λιθάζετε;
records.gloss: Answered them the Jesus, "Many works good I showed you from the Father; because of which of them work me do you stone?

L.32: Jesus answered them, "Many good works I have shown you from the Father; for which work of them are you stoning Me?"

R.32: But Jesus said to them, "I have done many good works for you to see. They all came from the Father. Which one of them are you going to stone Me for?"

decisions.choice: good: good in the sense of fine, noble, worth admiring
decisions.reason: The word is the one Jesus has just used of himself as "the good shepherd" (10:11, 14): what is good in itself and good to look at. The works are deeds such as the healings of 5:1-9 and 9:1-7, which showed the Father's goodness. The same word comes back in the reply of verse 33.

decisions.choice: from the Father: the works have their source in the Father
alternatives: done on the Father's behalf only
decisions.reason: Jesus does nothing on his own; the Father shows him what he does and gives him the works to complete (5:19-20, 36). In 10:25 he says the works he does in his Father's name testify about him, and in 10:37-38 he will rest his case on them.

decisions.choice: are you stoning me: an act begun but not completed
decisions.reason: The present tense describes what they are in the act of doing: they have the stones in their hands (verse 31) but have not thrown them. The question is pointed: for which good deed are they about to kill him?

decisions.choice: I have shown you: done before your eyes, so that you could see what they mean
decisions.reason: To "show" works is to do them openly as evidence. In 5:20 the Father shows the Son all that he does; here the Son has shown those works to them, and they still refuse to see.

decisions.choice: said to them (B, R); are you trying to stone (B); are you going to stone (R)
decisions.reason: Jesus "answers" what they do, not a question, so Balanced and Readable say "said". The verb form means an act under way (meaning decision m3); Balanced says "trying", Readable "going to".

decisions.choice: I have done many good works for you to see. They all came from the Father.
alternatives: I have shown you many good works from the Father
decisions.reason: Readable splits the clause and says what "shown you" means (meaning decision m4). It keeps the word "works", which recurs in verses 33, 37 and 38.

records.greek: ἀπεκρίθησαν αὐτῷ οἱ Ἰουδαῖοι· Περὶ καλοῦ ἔργου οὐ λιθάζομέν σε ἀλλὰ περὶ βλασφημίας, καὶ ὅτι σὺ ἄνθρωπος ὢν ποιεῖς σεαυτὸν θεόν.
records.gloss: Answered him the Jews, "For a good work not we stone you but for blasphemy, and because you a man being make yourself God."

L.33: The Jews answered Him, "For a good work we are not stoning You, but for blasphemy, and because You, who are a man, make Yourself God."

R.33: The Jews answered, "We are not stoning You for doing something good. We are stoning You because what You say is an insult to God. You are only a man, but You are making Yourself out to be God!"

decisions.choice: the Jews: the same hearers as in verse 31
alternatives: the Jewish people as a whole
decisions.reason: They answer the question Jesus has just put to them. They are the group who gathered around him in 10:24 and now hold stones (meaning decision on 10:31), not the people as a whole.

decisions.choice: blasphemy: speaking in a way that dishonors God; "and because" says what the blasphemy is
decisions.reason: The law put to death anyone who blasphemed the name of the LORD (Leviticus 24:10-16). The second clause does not add a new charge but explains the first: claiming to be God is, in their view, the blasphemy itself. Jesus repeats their charge in verse 36.

decisions.choice: make yourself God: God, the one God of Israel
decisions.reason: The word has no article, but Greek often leaves out the article with a noun that completes the verb, as here, and the same word without the article means God in 1:1 and 1:18. The charge matches 5:18, where they say he makes himself equal to God, and it answers what Jesus has just said: "I and the Father are one" (10:30). Grammar alone would also allow "a god", and Jesus's reply in verses 34-36 argues from "gods"; a footnote gives that reading.

decisions.choice: you, being a man, make yourself God: their charge, which John's reader sees in a different light
alternatives: a statement John endorses as it stands
decisions.reason: The reader knows from 1:1 and 1:14 that the Word was God and became flesh. So the speakers are right that a man stands before them and wrong about the rest: Jesus does not make himself anything. He does nothing on his own (5:19, 30), and it is the Father who glorifies him (8:54). Compare 5:18.

decisions.choice: It is not because of a good work ... It is because of blasphemy (B); two sentences (R)
decisions.reason: The Greek puts "for a good work" first for emphasis, throwing back Jesus's question. Balanced keeps the emphasis with "It is not ... It is"; Readable uses short sentences.

decisions.choice: what you say is an insult to God; making yourself out to be God
decisions.reason: Readable explains the word "blasphemy" (meaning decision m2) and says "making yourself out to be", which keeps the sense that this is a claim they reject (meaning decision m4).

records.greek: ἀπεκρίθη αὐτοῖς ὁ Ἰησοῦς· Οὐκ ἔστιν γεγραμμένον ἐν τῷ νόμῳ ὑμῶν ὅτι Ἐγὼ εἶπα· Θεοί ἐστε;
records.gloss: Answered them the Jesus, "Not is it written in the law of you that 'I said, Gods you are'?

L.34: Jesus answered them, "Does it not stand written in your law, 'I said, "You are gods"'?

R.34: Jesus answered them, "In your own law God says, 'I said, "You are gods."'

decisions.choice: your law (SBLGNT)
alternatives: the law, without "your" (a few early manuscripts)
decisions.reason: "Your" is missing from a few early witnesses, among them P45, the first hand of Codex Sinaiticus and Codex Bezae. Most manuscripts have it, and it matches 8:17 ("your law") and 15:25 ("their law"). The sense is hardly changed. A reviewer should check this against the apparatus.

decisions.choice: your law: the Scriptures as a whole, which you accept as God's word
alternatives: the five books of Moses only
decisions.reason: The words come from a psalm, not from the law of Moses, so "law" here means Scripture in general, as in 12:34 and 15:25 (both citing Psalms) and in Paul (1 Corinthians 14:21, citing Isaiah). "Your" is emphatic, as in 8:17: Jesus argues from the authority his hearers accept. He does not distance himself from it; verse 35 says it cannot be broken.

decisions.choice: Psalm 82:6: "I said, 'You are gods'"; God is the speaker, and those he calls gods are human beings who received his word, probably those entrusted with judging his people
alternatives: Israel as a whole, when it received the law at Sinai
decisions.reason: In Psalm 82 God stands among the "gods" and rebukes them for judging unjustly (82:1-4); then he says, "I said, 'You are gods, sons of the Most High, all of you'; but you will die like human beings" (82:6-7). The words quoted match the Greek Old Testament exactly. Jesus describes those addressed as people "to whom the word of God came" (10:35), which fits human hearers: rulers and judges who gave judgment in God's name (compare Exodus 22:8-9 and Psalm 82:2-4), or, as later rabbinic writings explain the psalm, Israel at Sinai. Because the psalm opens with God standing among the "gods" (82:1), it can also be read as addressed to heavenly beings. The argument in verses 35-36 works on any of these readings.

decisions.choice: Your own law says, does it not (B); In your own law God says (R)
alternatives: Does it not stand written in your law (Literal)
decisions.reason: The question expects the answer yes, which Balanced keeps with "does it not" and Readable turns into a statement. "Own" carries the emphatic "your" (meaning decision m2), as at 8:17. Readable names God as the speaker of "I said" (meaning decision m3).

records.greek: εἰ ἐκείνους εἶπεν θεοὺς πρὸς οὓς ὁ λόγος τοῦ θεοῦ ἐγένετο, καὶ οὐ δύναται λυθῆναι ἡ γραφή, ὃν ὁ πατὴρ ἡγίασεν καὶ ἀπέστειλεν εἰς τὸν κόσμον ὑμεῖς λέγετε ὅτι Βλασφημεῖς, ὅτι εἶπον· Υἱὸς τοῦ θεοῦ εἰμι;
records.gloss: If those he called gods to whom the word of the God came, and not is able to be broken the Scripture, \v 36 [of him] whom the Father consecrated and sent into the world you say that 'You blaspheme,' because I said, 'Son of the God I am'?

L.35: If He called those [people] gods to whom the word of God came, and the Scripture cannot be broken,
L.36: do you say of [Him] whom the Father consecrated and sent into the world, 'You are blaspheming,' because I said, 'I am [the] Son of God'?

R.35: God called them gods, the people who received His word. And no one can set aside what Scripture says.
R.36: The Father set Me apart for His work and sent Me into the world. So how can you say that I am insulting God because I said, 'I am the Son of God'?

decisions.choice: an argument from the lesser to the greater
alternatives: a claim that Jesus is a god only in the sense the psalm uses
decisions.reason: If Scripture, which cannot be wrong, could call mere human beings "gods" because God's word came to them, it cannot be blasphemy for the one whom the Father consecrated and sent into the world to call himself the Son of God. Jesus argued the same way in 7:23. The point is not that he is one of the psalm's "gods": he is greater than those who received the word, as the one the Father set apart and sent, and verse 38 goes on to say that the Father is in him and he in the Father.

decisions.choice: he called: God, the speaker of "I said" in the psalm
alternatives: it called: Scripture or the law
decisions.reason: In the psalm God says "I said, 'You are gods'" (10:34), so God is the natural subject. Since the psalm is Scripture, the sense is the same if the subject is taken to be the law.

decisions.choice: the word of God came to them: God spoke to them and gave them his word
